title: Strat Chat – Worked Examples/Think Alouds
author: Shaun Brien
summary: Shaun Brien, a Victorian VCE teacher, argues that teachers must make their thinking visible because expert knowledge hides the steps novices need. He warns of the educational rug pull in which students are taught facts but never taught how to apply them to unfamiliar questions, and insists that preparing students for the kinds of questions they will face is not teaching to the test. His remedy is worked examples and think-alouds, which he grounds in cognitive load theory with findings from Chen and colleagues and from Sweller and Cooper on faster, more accurate transfer to similar problems. He illustrates the method with a distinguish question from VCE Humanities and describes three ways to build an example: live on the whiteboard or visualiser, in the notes section of a slide deck for consistency across teachers, or animated into slides. He concludes that the planning investment pays off in independent practice because there should be no surprises for students.
points: The curse of knowledge means experts overestimate what novices infer from their explanations, so thinking has to be verbalised step by step.
Brien reframes preparing students for known question types as building knowledge and skill, not teaching to the test.
Two cited studies link worked examples to less processing time, fewer errors and better near-transfer to structurally different problems.
Three practical production methods are offered: live modelling with a visualiser, sample answers in slide notes for team consistency, and animated slides.
Overexplaining each element lets the teacher catch learners at their point of need, so independent practice holds no surprises.
quotes: Teachers can often make the mistake that we will teach students the knowledge, but never teach them how they are supposed to use that knowledge. The students end up with a binder full of facts which are amazing for short recall, but the moment that the knowledge needs to be applied to another context or with added complexity the students will hit a wall.

Making sure students are prepared for the types of questions they will definitely be assessed on is not “teaching to the test” it is building the knowledge and skills required for success. Preparing our students is not cheating.

How do we make our thinking visible to students? We model through worked examples and thinking aloud. This involves presenting students with a question similar to how they will be expected to apply their knowledge and then verbalizing step by step what you would do to create a high performing response.

It was found that not only did worked examples, as expected, require considerably less time to process than conventional problems, but that subsequent problems similar to the initial ones also were solved more rapidly. Furthermore, decreased solution time was accompanied by a decrease in the number of mathematical errors.

This is great for collective efficacy and consistency in language when one subject has many teachers. This also lessens your cognitive load as a teacher as you do not need to think about what needs to be included in the response while also doing the many other tasks a teacher needs to do to manage their class.

There is a sizeable amount of work in a worked example, but the investment of time and planning pays itself off significantly when it comes to student improvement in independent practice. There should be no surprises for students in education and using worked examples means that our students will be best prepared for whatever they face next.
